    In plain words

    Atlassian has released fixes for a serious weakness in self-hosted versions of products such as Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket. Someone who does not need to log in could potentially view certain files stored by an affected system if they already know the file’s exact name and location. Organizations running these products themselves should install the updates quickly or limit outside access, while customers using Atlassian’s cloud-hosted services do not need to act because the company has already fixed them.

    Summary
    Atlassian has issued urgent patches for CVE-2026-21589, a critical unauthenticated arbitrary file-access flaw affecting multiple self-hosted Data Center products including Jira, Confluence, and Bitbucket. Administrators should update immediately or restrict external access and deploy the documented temporary mitigations; Atlassian Cloud instances are already patched.

    Atlassian has warned customers about CVE-2026-21589, a critical arbitrary file-access vulnerability affecting multiple self-hosted Data Center products, including Confluence, Jira, and Bitbucket. An unauthenticated attacker can access specific files in an affected application’s web root directory. Exploitation requires prior knowledge of a target file’s exact name and path, and the flaw does not allow directory contents to be listed.

    The affected products include Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Jira Software, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, and Fisheye versions released before Atlassian’s listed fixed releases. Atlassian urges administrators to install the updates immediately; Cloud customers need take no action because the company has already patched those products. If patching cannot happen immediately, Atlassian recommends restricting external access or applying documented WAF, proxy, Tomcat rewrite, or URL rewrite mitigations across every cluster node, including Bitbucket mirrors and mirror farm nodes.

    • The issue does not let attackers browse directory contents, but it can still expose files when an attacker already knows their exact names and locations.
    • Atlassian recommends limiting external access even for internet-facing systems that normally require users to sign in, because the flaw can be used without authentication.
    • Temporary protections must be applied to every cluster node, including Bitbucket mirrors and mirror farm nodes, or some parts of a deployment may remain exposed.
    • Although Atlassian has seen no evidence of active exploitation, it says it cannot determine whether individual customer systems were compromised, making local log review important.
    Key Points

    • 02The flaw can allow an unauthenticated attacker to access specific files in an affected application’s web root directory if the attacker knows the exact file name and path.
    • 03Affected products include Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Jira Software, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, and Fisheye Data Center releases prior to Atlassian’s listed fixed versions.
    • 04Atlassian urged administrators to install the security updates immediately, while Atlassian Cloud customers require no action because their products were patched automatically.
    • 05Atlassian said it has no evidence that CVE-2026-21589 is being exploited, but advised customers to review access logs and apply temporary network restrictions or filtering rules if they cannot patch immediately.

    In plain words

    Atlassian disclosed a serious weakness in eight self-hosted versions of its workplace software that can let anyone on the network read certain files without signing in, if they know the exact file location. Businesses and organizations that run these products on their own servers are affected, while Atlassian’s online cloud customers have already been protected. The risk is that exposed files may contain sensitive information, so organizations should install the available updates quickly or temporarily keep the systems off the public internet.

    Summary
    Atlassian disclosed CVE-2026-21589, a critical unauthenticated path-traversal flaw affecting eight self-hosted Data Center products that can expose known files in application directories. Organizations should immediately upgrade to fixed releases or restrict public access and apply temporary blocking rules.

    Atlassian disclosed CVE-2026-21589 on October 5, rating it 9.3 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0. The flaw affects eight self-hosted Atlassian Data Center products and lets an unauthenticated attacker read specific files from an application’s web root directory when the attacker knows the exact file name and path. Atlassian said sensitive files may be present in that directory in some configurations, though the advisory does not identify them.

    The affected products are Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, and Fisheye Data Center, and Atlassian published fixed versions for each. Its cloud products have already been patched, Bitbucket Cloud is not affected, and cloud customers do not need to act. Organizations that cannot upgrade should take instances offline where possible, restrict public network access, or apply temporary rules that block suspicious file-path patterns; Atlassian also recommends reviewing logs for those patterns.

    • The flaw does not allow attackers to browse directory contents, but it can still expose sensitive files when an attacker already knows an exact filename and path.
    • Atlassian’s temporary mitigations differ by product: all eight can use a web application firewall or reverse-proxy rule, while only certain products support Tomcat or Bitbucket-specific configuration changes.
    • The published fix information contains discrepancies, including conflicting Crowd 7.1 versions and a Bamboo version mismatch in the CVE record.
    • Atlassian recommends checking logs for suspicious encoded file-path patterns, but its advisory does not explain how to determine whether a matching request successfully returned a file.
    Key Points
    • 01Atlassian disclosed CVE-2026-21589, rated 9.3 out of 10, which allows unauthenticated attackers to read specifically known files in the web application root directories of eight self-hosted Data Center products.
    • 02Affected products are Bitbucket, Confluence, Jira Software, Jira Service Management, Bamboo, Crowd, Crucible, and Fisheye Data Center; Atlassian has published fixed versions for each.
    • 03Atlassian stated that its affected cloud products have already been patched, Bitbucket Cloud is not affected, and cloud customers need take no action.
    • 04Organizations unable to upgrade immediately should restrict publicly reachable instances from external network access or apply Atlassian's temporary URL-blocking rules.
    • 05Atlassian advises customers to review access logs for suspicious file-path requests, although it said it cannot confirm whether individual self-hosted instances were affected.

In plain words

Atlassian disclosed a serious flaw in many self-hosted versions of Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, and related products that can let an outsider read files without signing in. The affected products are widely used by organizations to manage work, documentation, source code, and user access. In some setups, the exposed files can contain login details for Atlassian Crowd, the system that manages users, potentially allowing an attacker to create accounts or gain administrator-level control.

Summary
CVE-2026-21589 is a critical pre-authentication arbitrary file-read flaw in shared Atlassian web-resource code affecting Jira, Confluence, Bitbucket, and other Data Center products. Attackers can use encoded path traversal to read application files such as Crowd credentials, potentially enabling administrative takeover where Crowd integration is exposed.

Atlassian issued an out-of-band critical advisory for CVE-2026-21589, an arbitrary file-access issue described in the article as a pre-authentication arbitrary file-read vulnerability. It affects versions prior to listed fixes across Bitbucket Data Center, Confluence Data Center, Jira Software and Jira Service Management Data Center, Bamboo Data Center, Crowd Data Center, Crucible, and Fisheye. The article attributes the broad impact to shared Atlassian web-resource functionality used by these products.

The researchers found that shared code converts double colons (::) into forward slashes, allowing path-traversal-style requests to reach files within an application’s Tomcat context. They demonstrated reading protected WEB-INF files, including Jira’s web.xml, through a resource-download route. In Jira environments integrated with Atlassian Crowd, the readable WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties file can contain a plaintext Crowd application password and server details; the article shows that those credentials can be used to perform Crowd user-management actions, including creating a user and adding it to the jira-administrators group.

  • The unusual use of double colons in Atlassian's suggested filtering rule directly reflected the vulnerable shared code's conversion of "::" into forward slashes.
  • Although the demonstrated file reading was limited to the Tomcat application context, it could still reach normally protected WEB-INF files, including configuration files.
  • The severity can vary by deployment: Jira instances configured to use Atlassian Crowd may store a Crowd application name, password, and server URL in a plaintext crowd.properties file under WEB-INF/classes.
  • Leaked Crowd application credentials can enable user-management actions such as listing users, creating a user, and adding that user to the jira-administrators group, though Crowd IP allowlisting may make direct access harder.
Key Points
  • 01Atlassian disclosed CVE-2026-21589 as an arbitrary file-access issue that the article describes as a pre-authentication arbitrary file-read vulnerability affecting multiple products.
  • 02The issue affects versions before specified fixes for Bitbucket Data Center, Confluence Data Center, Jira Software and Jira Service Management Data Center, Bamboo Data Center, Crowd Data Center, Crucible, and Fisheye.
  • 03The researchers identified shared web-resource code that replaces double colons with forward slashes, enabling path traversal payloads using sequences such as "..::".
  • 04The researchers demonstrated reading protected application files such as Jira's WEB-INF/web.xml, while noting that traversal was limited to the Tomcat application context.
  • 05In Jira deployments integrated with Atlassian Crowd, reading WEB-INF/classes/crowd.properties can expose a plaintext Crowd application password that can be used to access Crowd user-management functions.
OPEN SOURCE ↗
JUSTIFICATION

This is a detailed analysis of a critical pre-authentication file-read flaw affecting numerous widely deployed Atlassian Data Center products. The demonstrated chain can expose Crowd credentials and enable administrator-level access in relevant configurations, making prompt patching and exposure assessment highly important.

The FBI removed an Accenture contractor after the contractor reportedly did not install a security update on an FBI job-site system run by Oracle. A group called ShinyHunters allegedly used that weakness to obtain personal details belonging to thousands of FBI employees. The case shows how one missed update at an outside service provider can put a major government agency and its workforce at risk, and the FBI says its investigation may lead to more arrests.

Summary
The FBI removed an Accenture contractor after an unpatched Oracle PeopleSoft platform was allegedly exploited by ShinyHunters, exposing personal information of thousands of FBI employees.

The FBI removed an Accenture contractor after determining that a contractor failed to install a security patch issued for a third-party-managed platform. The incident allegedly enabled ShinyHunters to obtain personal details belonging to thousands of FBI employees through the bureau’s job portal. The FBI said it has taken steps to reduce further risk and protect its workforce.

Reuters reported that the platform was Oracle PeopleSoft, though the FBI did not publicly name the third-party organization. Google-owned Mandiant assessed that ShinyHunters exploited a bypass for CVE-2026-35273 by using URL encoding to evade a web application firewall rule protecting the vulnerable Environment Management Hub endpoint. The FBI said two ShinyHunters members have been arrested, that it is pursuing further leads with partners, and that more arrests are likely.

  • The FBI attributed the incident to a missed patch that had been explicitly issued to secure the third-party-managed platform, highlighting patch implementation as the stated failure point.
  • ShinyHunters reportedly bypassed a web application firewall rule through URL encoding, meaning the protective rule did not prevent access to the vulnerable Environment Management Hub endpoint.
  • The breach involved a platform managed by a third party, but the FBI said it removed the contractor after its review, showing that contractor actions had direct consequences for the agency.
  • The FBI said two ShinyHunters members have already been arrested and that additional arrests are likely as it pursues further leads.

In plain words

Hackers are using flaws in older versions of the Ninja Forms and WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce add-ons to take control of WordPress websites. The affected add-ons are used on hundreds of thousands of sites, and the attackers can add visible or hidden site-manager accounts, create a secret way to log in, and upload more harmful files. Website owners should update the add-ons, but sites that were already compromised need to be checked because removing the obvious malicious add-on may not remove the attackers’ hidden access.

Summary
Attackers are actively exploiting stored XSS flaws in outdated Ninja Forms and WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce plugins to install backdoors and create hidden WordPress administrator accounts. Site owners should update to Ninja Forms 3.15.4+ or WPC Product Bundles 8.6.7+ and investigate for existing compromise, as updating alone will not remove persistence mechanisms.

Hackers are exploiting stored cross-site scripting flaws in the Ninja Forms and WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce WordPress plugins to install backdoors and create rogue administrator accounts. The affected versions are Ninja Forms 3.15.3 and older, tracked as CVE-2026-94504, and WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce 8.6.6 and older, tracked as CVE-2026-93836. Patchstack identified activity against WPC Product Bundles users on October 4 and observed the same activity against Ninja Forms the next day.

The attackers place malicious JavaScript in WooCommerce order data or Ninja Forms submissions, where it runs when a logged-in administrator views the content. The script retrieves administrative authorization values and installs a malicious plugin disguised as “WP Smart Thumbnails,” then establishes multiple persistence methods including visible and hidden administrator accounts, a secret login URL, and an unauthenticated file manager. Administrators should update to WPC Product Bundles 8.6.7 or later and Ninja Forms 3.15.4 or later, but updates do not remove existing infections, so compromised sites should also be checked for hidden access mechanisms.

  • Although the flaws require an authenticated session, attackers can place malicious content in orders or form submissions and wait for a logged-in administrator to view it.
  • The use of the same JavaScript payload from imgcdn1[.]com against both plugins indicates that the same threat actor is behind the observed attempts.
  • Removing the fake “WP Smart Thumbnails” plugin may not end the compromise because separate auxiliary plugins preserve the hidden administrator account and secret login URL.
  • The hidden administrator account is fully privileged but does not appear in the WordPress user list, administrator filter, or displayed user totals, making routine dashboard checks insufficient.
  • Updating the affected plugins stops further exploitation but does not clean sites that have already been infected.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers are exploiting stored cross-site scripting flaws in Ninja Forms versions 3.15.3 and older and WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce versions 8.6.6 and older.
  • 02The attacks place malicious JavaScript in form submissions or WooCommerce order data, which runs when a logged-in WordPress administrator views the affected content.
  • 03The JavaScript installs a malicious plugin posing as “WP Smart Thumbnails” and creates administrator accounts, including one hidden from the WordPress dashboard user list.
  • 04The malicious components provide multiple ways to retain access, including a secret login URL that authenticates as the site’s oldest existing administrator and an unauthenticated file manager.
  • 05Administrators should upgrade to Ninja Forms 3.15.4 or later and WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce 8.6.7 or later, but updates do not remove an existing infection.

JUSTIFICATION

This is an active exploitation campaign targeting two widely used WordPress plugins, including Ninja Forms on more than 500,000 sites. The compromise can create hidden administrator accounts and other persistent access paths that remain after the apparent malicious plugin is removed.

In plain words

People who were not authorized used a Danish company’s allowed access to look up personal records for about 8.8 million people in Denmark, including living people, those who moved abroad, and those who have died. The information included names, addresses, and personal ID numbers, although protected names and addresses were not included. This could make scams and identity fraud more convincing, so authorities are investigating and advising people not to share passwords, one-time codes, or card details with unexpected callers or messages.

Summary
Unauthorized actors used a Danish company’s legitimate access to the Central Person Register to retrieve names, addresses, and CPR data for roughly 8.8 million people. Authorities have revoked the access, launched an investigation, and urged residents to watch for targeted fraud and enable credit warnings.

Unauthorized parties used a private Danish company’s legitimate access to Denmark’s Central Person Register (CPR) to obtain names, addresses, and personal identification numbers for approximately 8.8 million people. The affected records include living residents, people who moved abroad, deceased people, and others, representing about four in five of the roughly 11 million people in the register. The Ministry of Digitalization said the figure is not yet final and that protected names and addresses were not included.

The access lasted about 10 days in September and was detected after a register administration employee noticed unusual activity on October 2. Datatilsynet said a very large number of automated lookups were made to identify valid CPR numbers, while authorities have not said how the unauthorized parties accessed the company’s systems, whether they retained or used the data, or who they are. The company’s access has been stopped, police and Datatilsynet are investigating, and residents are being urged to watch for convincing scams, avoid sharing MitID or payment details, and consider setting a credit warning through borger.dk.

  • The affected total represents about four in five of the approximately 11 million people recorded in the register, because it includes former residents and deceased people as well as current residents.
  • A credit warning does not prevent lending automatically: it signals participating companies to perform extra identity checks, and it may take several days to reach their systems.
  • Companies are supposed to receive register data only for people they have already identified, yet the article says the lookups covered roughly 8.8 million records; officials have not explained how that occurred under the access rules.
  • A CPR number is intended to help identify a person but, according to official guidance, should not be used as the only proof of identity.
Key Points
  • 01Unauthorized parties accessed names, addresses, and personal identification numbers for approximately 8.8 million people in Denmark’s Central Person Register through a private company’s legitimate lookup access.
  • 02The unauthorized access lasted about 10 days in September, and unusual activity was detected by a register administration employee on October 2.
  • 03The register administration stopped the company’s access, reported the incident to Denmark’s data protection authority, Datatilsynet, and police are investigating.
  • 04The accessed data did not include the names and addresses of people who had registered name-and-address protection, according to the Ministry of Digitalization.
  • 05Authorities advise people to be alert to unexpected messages and calls, never share MitID information or one-time codes, and consider setting a credit warning through borger.dk.

Blinder Tunnel Campaign Targets Iraqi Infrastructure
unit42.paloaltonetworks.com · 06 Oct 2026 10:00 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.6-terra
TAGSappdomainmanager-hijackingblackwoodchiselcl-sta-1178dll-sideloadingdubai-airportsgithub-apiiraniraqisraelmalicious-csprojmicrosoft-visual-studioshelbyc2-v2shelbyloader-v2united-arab-emirates

In plain words

Researchers say an Iran-linked group posed as Dubai Airports recruiters to trick an Iraqi software professional into opening a fake coding test for a job application. Opening the test could secretly install tools that let the attackers control the computer, hide their activity, and create a pathway into the victim’s organization’s internal network. The campaign targeted valuable infrastructure in Iraq and was also linked to credential-stealing lures aimed at an Israeli organization, showing how fake recruitment and familiar online services can be used to reach critical organizations.

Summary
Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 reports that an Iranian state-aligned cluster, CL-STA-1178, targeted Iraqi critical infrastructure by posing as Dubai Airports recruiters and delivering a malicious Visual Studio coding challenge. The campaign used AppDomainManager hijacking, DLL sideloading, GitHub-based command-and-control, and a custom Chisel tunneling loader to gain covert access and enable network pivoting.

Unit 42 identified the Blinder Tunnel campaign, tracked as CL-STA-1178, which targeted Iraqi critical infrastructure in March 2026 after infrastructure preparation beginning in November 2025. The researchers assess with high confidence that the activity aligns with an Iranian state-aligned threat actor and connect it to earlier Peaky Blinders-themed activity described as The Shelby Strategy. The attackers impersonated Dubai Airports IT recruiters and targeted a likely Iraqi software engineer with a fake career portal and a personalized coding challenge.

The coding challenge contained a weaponized Visual Studio project that executed malware when opened, using a malicious .csproj file, AppDomainManager hijacking, and DLL sideloading. The resulting tool set included ShelbyLoader V2, the ShelbyC2 V2 remote-access payload, a PowerShell execution module, and Blackwood, which loaded the Chisel tunneling tool in memory to create encrypted connections into compromised networks. The malware used GitHub repositories and GitHub Issues for command-and-control and fallback instructions, while attacker mistakes involving exposed infrastructure, reused servers, and embedded music metadata helped link the campaign to a separate credential-harvesting operation targeting an Israeli entity.

  • The malicious Visual Studio project could run the attackers’ code as soon as it was opened, during Visual Studio’s routine background project evaluation, before the target compiled or ran the apparent coding test.
  • The fake Dubai Airports career portal did not steal data or contact a remote server; the article says this harmless behavior was intended to make the later malicious coding challenge seem credible.
  • The malware used GitHub not only for its main communications but also as a backup channel, hiding encrypted replacement connection details inside comments on otherwise ordinary GitHub issues.
  • The attackers’ operational mistakes, including publicly exposed tooling, reused infrastructure, and Iranian music-site metadata left in an embedded song file, helped Unit 42 link the activity to an Iranian nexus and to a separate credential-harvesting campaign against an Israeli entity.
Key Points
  • 01Unit 42 tracks the Blinder Tunnel activity as CL-STA-1178 and assesses with high confidence that it was conducted by an Iranian state-aligned threat actor targeting Iraqi critical infrastructure in March 2026.
  • 02The attackers impersonated Dubai Airports IT recruiters and sent a weaponized Visual Studio coding challenge that executed malicious code when the victim opened the project.
  • 03The infection chain used a malicious .csproj project file, AppDomainManager hijacking, and DLL sideloading to launch the ShelbyLoader V2 malware while disabling Windows event tracing.
  • 04ShelbyLoader V2 used GitHub repositories and GitHub Issues as command-and-control channels to obtain commands, payload decryption material, and fallback connection details.
  • 05The campaign deployed Blackwood, a custom in-memory loader for the Chisel tunneling tool, to create encrypted network tunnels and enable access to compromised internal networks.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a detailed report on a named, Iranian-aligned espionage campaign targeting Iraqi critical infrastructure, with a concrete social-engineering delivery method, malware analysis, command-and-control infrastructure, and actionable indicators of compromise. It is especially relevant to organizations protecting developer workstations, critical infrastructure, or Middle Eastern operations.

South Korean officials believe AI agents were used to hack several banks

In plain words

South Korean authorities are investigating break-ins at at least seven financial companies that exposed personal information from at least 68,000 people, including names, phone numbers, income details, and borrowing histories. Officials believe a Chinese AI tool called Artex AI may have helped carry out the intrusions, including at banks such as Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, and Shinhan Bank. The case matters because officials say AI can now make it easier for people without deep technical skills to break into important systems, creating wider risks for banks and their customers.

Summary
South Korean authorities are investigating breaches at at least seven financial institutions that exposed data on roughly 68,000 people and may have involved the Chinese AI cybersecurity tool Artex AI. Officials say the case could represent an early example of AI agents being used to compromise the financial sector.

South Korean authorities are investigating breaches at at least seven financial institutions that reportedly exposed the personal data of at least 68,000 people. Officials believe the Chinese cybersecurity tool Artex AI was used in the intrusions, and President Lee Jae Myung said signs suggest AI agents were deployed in at least some attacks. Affected companies include Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank, and Shinhan Bank, which reportedly said information belonging to about 25,000 customers was exposed.

The compromised data included names, phone numbers, income information, and borrowing histories. Financial authorities identified 33 IP addresses connected to the incidents, linked to at least 12 countries including Japan, the United States, Thailand, Vietnam, and Hong Kong. The National Office of Investigation created a 28-person team to investigate, while Lee said the government would devote staff and funding to reduce the harm from the breaches.

In plain words

Criminals are taking over websites and showing visitors fake error messages, CAPTCHA checks, or browser-update prompts that tell them to copy and run a command on their own computer. The trick hides harmful code in the web browser’s temporary stored files, allowing a short pasted command to unlock a longer program that can steal browser and device credentials. Anyone who visits an affected site and follows the instructions can be harmed, while the growing availability of ready-made scam tools is making these campaigns more common.

Summary
A new ClickFix campaign uses compromised websites to pre-stage malicious scripts in browser cache files, letting attackers bypass Windows Run command-length limits when victims paste a fake CAPTCHA or troubleshooting command. The payload chain can steal browser and device credentials, highlighting the need to treat any verification prompt requesting commands in Run, PowerShell, or Terminal as malicious.

Microsoft reported a ClickFix campaign in which compromised websites place a malicious script in a visitor’s browser cache while disguising it as a PNG image. Victims are then shown a fake CAPTCHA, error, or other troubleshooting prompt that tells them to paste a command into the Windows Run dialog. Instead of directly downloading a payload, the command retrieves the script already cached on the device.

The method lets attackers work around the Windows Run dialog’s approximately 260-character input limit because the pasted command can be short while the larger payload remains in the cache. In the observed chain, a VBScript searches browser-profile cache files for one with a matching size, copies it to a temporary file with a .vbs extension, and runs it through wscript.exe. The subsequent stages collect host information, download PowerShell payloads, load .NET assemblies into memory, inject code into timeout.exe, and target browser and device credentials.

ClickFix campaigns are increasingly common because they persuade users to execute commands themselves through tools they already trust, including Run, PowerShell, and Terminal. The article also describes use of ClickFix by groups such as Stardust Chollima and Sandworm, as well as campaigns using compromised WordPress sites and EtherHiding to rotate lure infrastructure. Microsoft recommends web and network protections, application control, PowerShell script-block logging, and monitoring for suspicious browser activity, RunMRU entries, WScript or PowerShell child processes, and scheduled tasks.

  • The campaign selects the cached payload by matching its file size rather than searching its contents for a marker, and the expected size differs between variants.
  • Because the harmful script is already stored in the browser cache, attackers can use a short pasted command to work around the Windows Run dialog’s approximately 260-character limit.
  • ClickFix instructions can be inserted invisibly into HTML so that automated AI summarizers, but not human readers, process them and may produce attacker-controlled instructions in their summaries.
  • Attackers can use EtherHiding to rotate the active fake-lure website through blockchain updates without changing the code on a compromised website.
  • Microsoft recommends hunting beyond download activity for suspicious browser behavior, RunMRU registry entries, WScript or PowerShell child processes, and scheduled tasks.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft reported a ClickFix technique in which compromised websites pre-fetch a malicious script into browser cache disguised as a PNG file, then prompt victims to execute a command that uses the cached content.
  • 02The approach bypasses the Windows Run dialog’s roughly 260-character input limit by having a short command locate a cache file of a specified size, copy it to a temporary VBScript file, and run it with wscript.exe.
  • 03In the observed chain, the VBScript collects host information, retrieves PowerShell scripts and additional payloads, and ultimately loads .NET code into memory to target browser and device credentials.
  • 04ClickFix lures commonly use fake CAPTCHAs, browser updates, or error messages to persuade users to paste attacker-supplied commands into trusted tools such as Windows Run, PowerShell, or Terminal.
  • 05Microsoft recommends cloud-delivered, web, and network protection, application control, PowerShell script-block logging, and hunting for suspicious browser activity and RunMRU, WScript, PowerShell, and scheduled-task indicators.

JUSTIFICATION

The technique is actionable for defenders because it identifies concrete hunting signals, including browser-cache activity, RunMRU entries, WScript/PowerShell child processes, and scheduled tasks.

    In plain words

    Scammers have created convincing websites that pretend to offer advertising tools from AI brands such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude. When agency employees or advertising-account managers try to connect an account, the sites show fake sign-in pages that steal their passwords and one-time verification codes. The criminals can then take control of business advertising accounts, spend the company’s money on their own ads, or sell trusted accounts to others. Recovering control can take weeks or months, and agencies may also put their clients’ accounts at risk.

    Summary
    A phishing platform is impersonating AI advertising tools for ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and other brands to steal business-account credentials and MFA codes through fake browser login windows. The campaign targets advertising agencies and account administrators, enabling attackers to hijack valuable ad accounts for fraudulent spending or resale.

    Researchers at Island identified a human-operated phishing platform that impersonates advertising products for AI brands including Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Perplexity, Meta Muse, and Manus. The fake services claim to offer functions such as campaign optimization, advertising-spend audits, and business-account connections. They are designed to steal credentials and multi-factor authentication codes from agency staff, media buyers, and advertising manager-account administrators.

    Clicking a “Connect” button opens a counterfeit sign-in window inside the real browser, with a fake address bar displaying trusted domains such as accounts.google.com or an Okta tenant. The platform fingerprints the victim’s device, sends data through Socket.IO, and lets an operator choose the next authentication challenge while attempting to access the account in real time. Stolen advertising accounts can be used to run fraudulent ads or sold for profit, and attackers may add their own administrators and reduce the legitimate owner’s access, making recovery take weeks or months.

    • The phishing operation rapidly adapts its branding to current AI news, with museads.ai appearing shortly after Meta launched Muse.
    • Rather than using one generic lure, the platform gives each impersonated AI brand a tailored advertising pitch, such as Google Ads briefs, manager-account support, spend audits, or private Meta integrations.
    • The platform supports real-time account takeover: after collecting login details, attackers attempt to sign in immediately and can choose the next verification challenge shown to the victim.
    • For advertising accounts, removing a payment card may be quick, but attackers can add their own administrators and reduce the legitimate owner’s access, making recovery take weeks or months.
    • The same underlying platform also supports Google Ads refund and payment lures and fake recruitment sites for brands including Tesla, Louis Vuitton, Nike, and Adecco.
    Key Points
    • 01Researchers identified a human-operated phishing platform that impersonates advertising products for AI chatbots including Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, OpenAI ChatGPT, Perplexity, Meta Muse, and Manus.
    • 02The fake sites use a browser-within-a-browser trick to display counterfeit login windows with trusted-looking address bars and capture account credentials and multi-factor authentication codes.
    • 03The platform fingerprints victims’ devices, sends the information to an attacker-controlled endpoint, and allows an operator to choose which authentication challenge the victim sees next.
    • 04The campaign targets agency staff, media buyers, and advertising manager-account administrators, and attackers may monetize stolen advertising accounts by running campaigns or selling accounts with clean spending histories.
    • 05The identified sites share a Next.js and Socket.IO technology stack, and earlier platform source code was exposed through misconfigured public GitHub repositories.

Malicious spreadsheets can exploit automatic database-range refreshes and Java JDBC drivers to execute code in LibreOffice and Apache OpenOffice without macro warnings. LibreOffice fixed the issue in versions 26.2.5 and 26.8.0, while OpenOffice users should disable Java or avoid untrusted files until 4.1.17 is released.

Researchers demonstrated that a malicious spreadsheet can cause LibreOffice and Apache OpenOffice to run attacker-controlled code when the file is opened, without displaying the warning normally shown before macros run. The issue requires Java support to be enabled and has so far only been demonstrated as a proof of concept, with no reported real-world exploitation. The technique was tested on Windows and Linux.

The spreadsheets use an automatically refreshed database range to retrieve an external database file, which can specify a Java database driver and where its code is located. The applications can then download and start that Java code inside the office program. LibreOffice fixed CVE-2026-63277 in versions 26.2.5 and 26.8.0, while Apache OpenOffice’s CVE-2026-59265 remains unfixed through version 4.1.16; users can disable Java or avoid untrusted spreadsheets until the expected 4.1.17 release.

  • There are no reported cases of the flaw being used in real attacks so far, despite a public proof of concept being available.

In plain words

Researchers found hidden programs on Linux-based telecom and network devices in South Korea and Taiwan that pretend to be trusted email-security software or ordinary system processes. These programs can quietly contact their operators, let them browse or copy files, run commands, and route connections through the infected device. This matters because telecom networks and email gateways handle sensitive communications, so attackers can use access to these systems for spying or to maintain a hidden foothold in important infrastructure.

Summary
Rapid7 found Linux backdoors targeting telecom and edge appliances in South Korea and Taiwan that impersonate regional email-security tools and legitimate processes to evade detection. The BPFDoor, Rekoobe, and newly identified AVERAT implants use stealthy packet triggers or SMTP-based command-and-control to enable persistent remote access, file transfer, proxying, and data theft.

Rapid7 identified Linux backdoors targeting telecom and network appliances in South Korea and Taiwan that disguise themselves as familiar email-security products and ordinary Linux processes. The activity includes a new BPFDoor variant and a BPF Rekoobe build impersonating SpamSniper components in South Korea, as well as the previously unreported AVERAT implant deployed on Taiwanese ShareTech appliances. The disguises include SpamSniper-related PID and process names, as well as an Oracle-like process name, ora_ppmond.

BPFDoor uses Berkeley Packet Filter functionality to watch incoming traffic and activate only after a trigger packet is received; newer samples can receive that trigger in standard HTTPS POST requests. Once active, it can launch TinyShell for interactive command execution and file transfers, while the Rekoobe-based backdoor monitors network traffic associated with port 25. AVERAT contacts its command server over TCP port 25 and supports file transfers, interactive shells, process management, rebooting, shared-object modules, and proxy or port-forwarding channels. Rapid7 recommended reviewing unexpected raw packet sockets and BPF filters, auditing unusual outbound port 25 connections, checking for disguised daemon processes, and restricting management access to edge appliances.

  • The backdoors use regionalized disguises by copying names associated with SpamSniper in South Korea and ShareTech appliances in Taiwan, rather than relying only on generic Linux process names.
  • BPFDoor operators adapted after static network signatures were created by placing their trigger within ordinary HTTPS POST requests, taking advantage of SSL offloading common in telecom environments.
  • AVERAT’s installer derives an encryption key from the literal string "ShareTech," decrypts a shell script, and deletes both the installer and payload files 10 seconds after deployment.
  • Because AVERAT communicates through TCP port 25, outbound SMTP connections from processes that are not legitimate mail services are a specifically useful detection opportunity.

  • 02The South Korea-focused activity includes a new BPFDoor variant and a BPF Rekoobe build that impersonate SpamSniper components, while a separate campaign deployed the previously unreported AVERAT implant on Taiwanese ShareTech appliances.
  • 03BPFDoor uses Berkeley Packet Filter functionality to monitor incoming traffic and activates after receiving a specific trigger, with newer variants able to receive that trigger inside standard HTTPS POST requests.
  • 04AVERAT uses SMTP for command-and-control, periodically contacting mx.zxopfds[.]com over TCP port 25 and supporting commands for file transfers, process control, interactive shells, rebooting devices, and proxying connections.
  • 05Rapid7 recommended that organizations examine unexpected raw packet sockets and BPF filters, audit unusual outbound TCP port 25 traffic, look for processes impersonating common daemons, and restrict management access to edge appliances.

Alleged Ploutus ATM-malware developer Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre pleaded not guilty in Nebraska after being returned to the United States, where he faces charges tied to a jackpotting scheme that allegedly stole more than $5.4 million. U.S. authorities link the operation to Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua and say Aguirre could face up to 70 years in prison if convicted.

Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre, a Venezuelan national also known as “Prometheus” and “The Engineer,” pleaded not guilty in a Nebraska federal court and will remain detained pending trial. The FBI alleges that Aguirre was the mastermind behind Ploutus, software used to make ATMs dispense their cash. He was added to the FBI’s Top 10 Most Wanted Fugitives list in March as the first cybercriminal included on it. The Justice Department has not disclosed when or where he was detained, and said he was returned to the United States without extradition.

Authorities allege that participants physically opened ATMs, connected personal devices, and installed Ploutus, while Aguirre remotely directed aspects of the operation. The group allegedly conducted 117 ATM jackpotting incidents from February 2024 through December 2025, stealing more than $5.4 million from banks and credit unions, often by targeting machines in remote locations. Aguirre faces charges including bank fraud conspiracy, bank burglary conspiracy, computer-related fraud, money laundering, and providing material support to terrorists, carrying a potential maximum sentence of 70 years. Officials also allege that proceeds were laundered through cryptocurrency and businesses in Mexico and elsewhere, with links to the Venezuelan criminal group Tren de Aragua.

The case is part of a broader crackdown in which 120 people have been charged in the ATM jackpotting scheme. U.S. officials have recorded at least 1,500 ATM jackpotting attacks with $40.7 million in losses. Ploutus variants have been used against ATMs in Latin America and the United States since 2013, though researchers tracking the software have not verified that Aguirre is its actual developer. Treasury sanctioned Aguirre and several others last week for allegedly using businesses and other methods to launder scheme proceeds.

Summary
Google has temporarily stopped accepting reward-eligible product vulnerability reports for its open-source projects, including Go and Angular, after a surge in mostly invalid automated submissions. Supply-chain compromise reports and other reward programs remain available while Google reworks the OSS VRP, with an update planned by Q1 2027.

Google has temporarily paused reward-eligible product vulnerability reports for its Open Source Software Vulnerability Reward Program (OSS VRP), effective October 1. The company said the move followed a significant rise in automated submissions, the vast majority of which were invalid. The pause affects flaws in Google-maintained open-source projects such as Go, Angular, Flutter, Bazel, and Protocol Buffers, while reports filed before October 1 are unaffected.

Supply-chain compromise reports, including issues that could permit tampering with a project’s source code or published packages, remain eligible for rewards. Researchers may also be able to use the Cloud VRP for certain Google Cloud repositories, submit accepted fixes through the Patch Rewards Program, or report issues through other applicable Google reward programs. Google removed previously listed product-vulnerability reward amounts from its rules and said it will provide an update in the first quarter of 2027, but did not state when submissions will resume or whether unrewarded reports will still be accepted.

  • Google removed the published product-vulnerability reward amounts from its public rules on September 30, one day before publicly announcing the pause.
  • The pause does not clearly state whether Google will continue to accept product vulnerability reports without paying a reward.
  • Researchers who submit patches through Google’s Patch Rewards Program must have the patch accepted by maintainers and keep it in place for one month before submitting it for payment.
  • Google had already tightened evidence requirements for some OSS VRP reports in March 2026, and the Go project later warned that unreviewed reports generated by large language models would not be credited.
  • Angular’s published security policy still directs reporters to the OSS VRP and does not list another reporting channel, despite the program’s product-vulnerability pause.

Summary
Osaka Metropolitan University canceled classes and took much of its IT environment offline after a suspected ransomware incident disrupted roughly 500 servers. Osaka Metropolitan University canceled classes and shut down much of its IT infrastructure after a suspected ransomware incident that began late last week. The outage made its internal network, email, websites, and systems for academic administration, educational support, financial accounting, payroll, human resources, and library services unavailable. The university said it is investigating with outside cybersecurity specialists and has not identified the attackers or said whether it received a ransom demand.

Japanese media reported that around 500 servers stopped operating and that information belonging to at least 130,000 current and former students, faculty members, and other affiliated people may have been exposed. The university has not confirmed that personal data was stolen and has reported the incident to Japan’s data protection authority and other government agencies. In-person classes were planned to resume Friday, while online classes depended on system recovery; externally hosted admissions systems, the university hospital’s electronic medical record system, and the veterinary clinical center remained operational.

  • The incident disrupted a broad set of university functions at once, but externally hosted entrance exam and enrollment systems remained available, indicating that those services were not affected by the university’s internal outage.
  • The university hospital’s electronic medical record system and veterinary clinical center continued operating despite the wider disruption, limiting the impact on medical and veterinary services.
  • Potentially affected information may include records tied to Osaka Prefecture University and Osaka City University, which merged to form Osaka Metropolitan University in 2022, extending the possible exposure beyond the current university population.
  • The university had not confirmed data theft or identified the attackers at the time of reporting, despite reports that information on at least 130,000 people may have been exposed.

OX Security’s analysis of 15,465 publicly indexed MCP servers found widespread governance gaps, including servers hosted in unapproved jurisdictions, personal-machine tunnels, and dangling domains vulnerable to takeover. Organizations should independently vet MCP server provenance, hosting, and ongoing integrity rather than relying on marketplace listings or public repositories.

OX Security analyzed 15,465 publicly indexed Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers across five registries, reducing them to 5,095 unique hostnames. The company says MCP marketplaces lack required vetting or an automated pre-publication scanner comparable to Google’s former Android Bouncer. It also cautions that reviewing a public repository does not verify what a remote MCP server runs, because backend code can differ from publicly shown code.

The analysis found that 15.6% of hostnames resolved to infrastructure outside the United States, including 19 in China and 18 in Russia. It found that 0.45% routed traffic through consumer tunneling services, mainly ngrok-free, while 2.3% no longer resolved and six used expired domains that could be re-registered. OX Security says MCP connections can sit outside enterprise controls such as data-residency rules, access boundaries, and supply-chain audits, and calls for vetting, code signing, and origin verification.

  • Reviewing a public code repository cannot confirm what a remote MCP server actually runs, because its backend code may differ from the code shown publicly.

  • An expired MCP server domain can be re-registered by a new owner, who could inherit the server’s established identity and receive requests from agents still configured to use it.
  • Enterprise cloud controls such as data-residency rules, access boundaries, and supply-chain audits may not cover MCP connections, even when those connections handle enterprise data.

Employees at an Austrian airline-catering and hospitality company received fake HR attendance reports that looked like routine paperwork and included a QR code leading to an unrelated German website. Summary
A phishing campaign used a convincing fake HR attendance PDF with a QR code to an unrelated domain, but exposed itself by repeatedly using recipients’ email addresses where employee names should appear. The clean-scoring attachment and link were reported by an employee, enabling all delivered copies to be removed.

A first-time external sender delivered a PDF posing as a monthly HR attendance report to four employees at an Austrian airline-catering and gourmet-hospitality group. The document greeted recipients as “Team Member” and repeatedly inserted each recipient’s email address into fields intended for an employee name. It included a detailed but invented leave-code legend and plausible attendance times, attempting to resemble routine internal paperwork.

The PDF contained a QR code labeled as a way to view full attendance details online, directing recipients to an unrelated German domain. Both the attachment and the QR-derived link received clean verdicts, while the QR destination was not displayed in the email client and could be scanned from a phone. The email body itself contained no attacker-written prose, instead rendering Microsoft’s first-contact notice and the organization’s external-sender warning banner.

An employee reported the message, and all four delivered copies were permanently deleted. The article argues that external messages presenting internal HR, payroll, or attendance records should be treated as forged, particularly when they use an email address instead of an employee’s name or direct recipients to an unrelated domain. It identifies the campaign as spearphishing via attachment and emphasizes that routine-looking paperwork without urgency can still be deceptive.

  • The campaign deliberately avoided urgency, payment demands, and follow-up requests, showing that a message framed as routine “for your records” paperwork can bypass checks that focus on pressure tactics.
  • The attacker provided no message-body text; the only rendered prose outside the attachment was Microsoft’s first-contact notice and the recipient organization’s own external-sender warning banner.
  • A fake opt-out instruction embedded inside the PDF can resemble a legitimate subscription control while avoiding checks that rely on actual email unsubscribe headers.
  • The QR code was embedded as a page-one image, so its destination was not displayed in the email client and could lead recipients to use a phone outside the organization’s email protections.
  • The article identifies a simple screening signal independent of file or website reputation: an external sender cannot legitimately issue an organization’s own internal HR record, especially when it directs employees to an unrelated domain.
Key Points

  • 02The PDF repeatedly used each recipient’s email address in fields intended for an employee name and greeted recipients as “Team Member,” indicating that the sender lacked actual employee information.
  • 03The PDF contained a QR code directing recipients to an unrelated German domain for purported full attendance details, while both the attachment and QR-derived link received clean verdicts.
  • 04An employee reported the message, and the record shows that all four delivered copies were permanently deleted.
  • 05The article recommends treating externally sent HR, payroll, or attendance documents that use an email address instead of an employee name as forged.

Summary
Former infrastructure engineer Daniel Rhyne was sentenced to 32 months in prison for locking thousands of his employer’s Windows devices, deleting admin accounts, and demanding 20 Bitcoin in an extortion scheme.

Former core infrastructure engineer Daniel Rhyne, 57, was sentenced to 32 months in prison for an extortion plot against the New Jersey-based industrial company that employed him. He remotely accessed its network without authorization and locked thousands of devices in a ransomware-style incident. The disruption affected 254 servers and 3,284 workstations after administrator passwords were changed. Rhyne had pleaded guilty following his August 2024 arrest.

Between November 8 and November 25, 2023, Rhyne used an administrator account and scheduled tasks to change passwords, delete 13 domain administrator accounts, and change passwords for 301 domain users. He also shut down random servers and workstations over several days in December 2023. In a November 25 email titled “Your Network Has Been Penetrated,” he demanded 20 Bitcoin, claimed backups had been deleted, and threatened to shut down 40 random servers each day for ten days if the company did not pay. Investigators found searches on his hidden virtual machine and laptop for instructions related to changing passwords, deleting accounts, clearing Windows logs, and remotely shutting down computers.

  • The disruption did not require reported data encryption: password changes and deletion of administrator accounts alone denied access to 254 servers and 3,284 workstations.
  • The scheduled tasks targeted both domain-level and local administrator accounts, allowing the lockout to affect central network management as well as individual servers and workstations.
  • Investigators linked pre-incident web searches from Rhyne’s hidden virtual machine and laptop to the specific actions used in the extortion plot, including password changes, account deletion, log clearing, and remote shutdowns.
  • The ransom email combined a payment demand with claims that backups had been deleted and a threat to shut down 40 servers each day, increasing pressure on the employer to pay.

Socket has launched experimental scanning for more than 100,000 VS Code Marketplace extensions to help organizations detect risky or malicious behaviors before installation or automatic updates. The move follows incidents such as the compromised Nx Console update and Socket’s GlassWorm investigation, which showed extensions can steal code, download payloads, and execute processes.

Socket has launched experimental scanning for VS Code Marketplace extensions, adding coverage for more than 100,000 extensions alongside its existing Open VSX coverage. The service is intended to help teams assess extensions before adopting them, including the tools developers use in environments containing source code, credentials, and company infrastructure. Socket says its analysis examines extension code, dependencies, activation patterns, and capabilities such as file access, network activity, process execution, bundled executables, obfuscation, and hidden functionality.

The announcement highlights the risk of malicious extension updates, noting GitHub’s disclosure that a poisoned update to the legitimate Nx Console extension on an employee device led to the exfiltration of internal repositories. Socket also cites its GlassWorm investigation, which connected four VS Code Marketplace extensions and six Open VSX extensions, including two confirmed malicious extensions. One malicious theme used encrypted JavaScript and a Solana dead drop to locate and execute additional payloads, demonstrating that even apparently harmless extensions can conceal harmful behavior.

  • Allowlisting an extension at installation is not sufficient by itself, because automatic updates can replace previously vetted code with malicious code while retaining the same extension name and publisher.

  • Reviewing an extension in isolation can miss campaign-level risk: Socket linked related GlassWorm extensions through code reuse, shared infrastructure, and publishing patterns, including extensions without active malicious payloads in the analyzed versions.
  • An extension’s activation behavior is a meaningful review factor because it determines when its executable code runs, alongside its access to files, network connections, and external processes.

AI tools are allowing non-technical employees to build workplace applications from natural-language prompts, improving productivity and reducing demands on professional developers. However, applications created without IT and security oversight can become shadow AI assets with security and compliance problems. They may contain untested vulnerabilities, dangerous configurations, risky open-source components, insecure connections to critical systems, or weak protection for sensitive data. Such applications may also lack patching, monitoring, logging, backups, disaster-recovery coverage, and appropriate access controls.

Tenable argues that blanket bans on AI-aided application development are likely to drive the activity underground rather than eliminate it. The company uses a five-tier AI governance model spanning executive strategy, governance bodies, departmental execution, training and enablement, and employee communities. Departmental AI Functional Leaders oversee AI use cases, requests for skills, connectors, and data access, helping identify unvetted external AI components before production. Tenable also links AI-tool access to mandatory security and responsible-use training, supplemented with webinars, courses, tool-specific instruction, and weekly show-and-tell sessions.

Silent Push 6.2 adds centralized organization, team, role, and per-user API access controls, while integrating its preemptive threat intelligence into ThreatConnect, Microsoft Sentinel, and Palo Alto Cortex XSOAR. Silent Push released version 6.2, adding centralized organization management controls for administrators, teams, managers, and members. Administrators can create teams, assign users, control module access, set daily and monthly API usage caps, and onboard users in bulk through a CSV template. The release is intended to provide access and usage governance as more security organizations adopt the platform.

The platform’s access model limits managers to their own team’s users and API keys, while members can see only their own keys. Permission changes make content unavailable but do not delete it, and removing a user who shared content prompts administrators to transfer ownership. On limited-tier plans, API caps are soft limits that display actual usage against configured limits, while limit flags can be disabled through the user interface or API.

Silent Push 6.2 also brings IOFA Threat Check and Traffic Origin Threat Check into ThreatConnect, Microsoft Sentinel through Microsoft Logic Apps, and Palo Alto Cortex XSOAR. IOFA Threat Check identifies IP addresses or domains connected to infrastructure flagged as a potential future threat, while Traffic Origin adds source IP, geographic, and traffic-pattern context. The Cortex XSOAR integration additionally includes Traffic Origin support and a TLP Amber Reports API for listing available restricted intelligence reports.

  • The access model is designed to scale from small organizations that manage users directly to larger organizations that need teams, delegated managers, and role-based visibility.
  • Configured API limits are described as soft controls on limited-tier plans, meaning they provide usage visibility rather than necessarily interrupting an analyst’s work.
  • Permission changes make content unavailable without deleting it, and removing a user triggers an ownership-transfer prompt for shared content, reducing the risk of losing investigation material.
  • The integrations combine an early-warning signal about potentially threatening infrastructure with source, geographic, and traffic-pattern context, allowing analysts to assess both whether an indicator may be dangerous and what it may be connected to.
  • Bulk CSV onboarding can assign per-user API limits during user creation, linking access provisioning with usage governance in one process.

This sponsored Acronis article argues that remote monitoring and management (RMM) software is a major attack surface for managed service providers because it gives technicians unattended administrative access across many customer devices. It cites N-able’s September 2026 emergency hotfix for CVE-2026-86218, a maximum-severity pre-authentication remote-code-execution flaw in N-central, and Microsoft SharePoint “ToolShell” zero-days exploited before a patch was available. The article also references a CISA warning that ransomware actors can abuse legitimate RMM software to reach downstream customer networks.

The article recommends testing eight RMM control areas: device discovery, risk-based patching, privileged-access restrictions, alert handling, secure scripting, security-operations integration, recovery readiness, and tenant separation with audit records. It advises MSPs to use difficult test cases, including unmanaged devices, failed patches, unauthorized scripts, restricted technician accounts, compromised test devices, and restores that still require updates. In plain words

The article explains how Aikido Security can help companies prepare evidence for SOC 2, an outside review of whether they protect their systems and information. It says the service can regularly check software, cloud settings, passwords accidentally exposed in code, and changes before they are released, while keeping a record of problems and fixes. This matters to companies seeking a SOC 2 report because a longer Type 2 review requires proof that safeguards kept working over months, not just that they existed on one day.

Summary
Aikido Security positions its continuous scanning, remediation tracking, CI/CD gates, and cloud posture checks as a way to generate audit evidence for SOC 2 controls. It emphasizes setting up these controls early for SOC 2 Type 2, which requires proof that controls operated effectively over time.

The article explains how Aikido Security can help organizations collect evidence for SOC 2 audits through its application and cloud-security platform. SOC 2 Type 1 evaluates whether controls are properly designed at a specific point in time, while Type 2 evaluates whether those controls worked effectively over a period, typically three to 12 months. The article emphasizes that Type 2 requires sustained records such as logs, timestamps, and remediation history rather than one-time configuration screenshots.

Aikido combines code, dependency, secret, container, infrastructure, cloud, malware, and application testing capabilities with remediation workflows and SLA tracking. It maps these capabilities to SOC 2 areas including access controls, boundary protection, encryption, software integrity, monitoring, vulnerability management, change management, risk assessment, and availability. The article says CI/CD gates can block pull requests or releases based on defined issue-severity thresholds and retain auditable records of gate decisions, overrides, and exceptions.

The article advises teams pursuing Type 1 with a near-term Type 2 goal to enable continuous scanning and SLA tracking before the formal audit period starts. It notes that Aikido alone cannot pass an audit, because auditors also require policies, procedures, risk assessments, access reviews, and incident-response processes. Its central claim is that a unified platform can reduce the effort of producing exportable evidence showing that security controls continuously detected and addressed issues during the audit window.

  • Teams preparing first for SOC 2 Type 1 should enable continuous scanning and remediation tracking before the Type 2 audit period begins, because evidence not captured during that period cannot be recreated later.
  • A vulnerability-management program can prioritize issues using whether vulnerable code is reachable or demonstrably exploitable in the company’s environment, rather than treating every dependency finding equally.
  • Pull-request and release gates can serve as change-management evidence when their decisions, exceptions, and overrides are retained in an auditable record.
  • Availability requirements are separate from the common criteria in SOC 2, so cloud backup-integrity checks can support availability evidence specifically.
Key Points
  • 01SOC 2 Type 1 assesses whether controls are appropriately designed at a specific point in time, while Type 2 evaluates whether controls operated effectively over a period typically lasting three to 12 months.
  • 02Aikido Security combines code, dependency, secret, container, infrastructure, cloud, malware, and application testing capabilities in one platform with remediation workflows and SLA tracking.
  • 03Continuous scanning and dated remediation records can provide Type 2 audit evidence showing that vulnerability-management controls operated throughout the audit period.
  • 04Aikido's CI/CD and source-control checks can block pull requests, builds, or releases when newly introduced issues meet an organization-defined severity threshold.
  • 05The article states that Aikido alone cannot pass a SOC 2 audit, because auditors also require policies, procedures, risk assessments, access reviews, and incident-response processes.

Phones, computers, or tablets owned by an individual rather than managed by an employer.
